newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian troops kill 300 rebels, trap more - papers.
newsitem.headline: Algerian troops kill 300 rebels, trap more - papers.

text.p: Troops backed by helicopters killed more than 300 Moslem rebels in a two-week offensive and now have scores more trapped in northeastern Algeria's mountains, Algerian newspapers said on Monday.

One newspaper quoted an army officer as warning civilians in villages, mainly south of Algiers, that Moslem guerrillas might stage more massacres and bomb attacks after rebel losses in a government offensive.
Hundreds of civilians have been killed in massacres and bomb attacks in towns and villages in the past two years when the country's strife took a more bloody turn.
More than 90 villagers, including childen, died in massacres last week in hamlets in Blida province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, and neighbouring Hadjout and Bou Smail areas.

One newspaper said last week that these were carried out to try to force the military to ease its stranglehold on rebels trapped in its offensive which began when a woman, kidnapped during an earlier massacre, escaped.
She tipped off authorities about a rebel hideout in Attatba area in Blida region.

Le Matin and Al Khabar dailies said on Monday that after the offensive there troops had moved to Sidi Bouzid, Magtaa Kheira and Oued el Alleug, south and west of Attatba, to encircle and pound scores more rebels holed up there.
One paper put the number of rebels at 50, another at 60.

"We encountered them here in this forest (in Magtaa Kheira)...The dogs wanted to flee into Oued el Alleug. They were firing and shouting 'Allahu Akbar' ('God is Greatest')," said Le Matin, quoting a government force member.
"We clashed with them all night and at dawn we put them under bombardment...," he added, talking about an unspecified number of rebels holed up in Magtaa Kheira.

Le Matin said security forces found 40 blockhouses in the area, each able to hold about 20 rebels. It said bulldozers guarded by soldiers began ploughing roads through the forest in the nearby Sidi Bouzid area.
"We will shell the area in the next few days," an army officer told Le Matin.

Reporting on the earlier offensive in which some papers said 150 rebels died, Le Matin on Monday said: "More than 300 terrorists, including Emirs (unit leaders), have been killed by the security forces in a huge operation since July 14."
One day after that operation began, Algerian authorities freed on parole their most senior Islamist prisoner, Abassi Madani, head of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

He was let out conditionally after serving only half a 12 year prison term imposed 12 months after his arrest in mid-1991, six months before his then-legal party swept to a huge lead in a general election which the authorities scrapped in January 1992.
Violence rapidly erupted and about 60,000 people have been killed since then.
Madani's release and the military crackdown appeared to follow a long-standing carrot-and-stick policy by Algerian authorities.
Over the years they have maintained a ruthless pursuit of armed Islamists while offering clemency to those who surrendered without blood on their hands.

Similarly, despite a ban on the use of Islam to attract votes they allowed two Islamist-leaning parties, including Nahda, to compete in last month's general election. The two won a total 103 seats in the 380-seat house.
Algeria said Madani's release was conditional, but on Monday, Abdallah Djaballah, leader of Nahda, was quoted in the Egyptian newspaper Al Ahram as saying Madani's had refused to sign terms.
Nor would he abide by the interior minister's order not to indulge in political activities without ministerial approval, said Djaballah.
Meanwhile, in an apparent return to killing of personalities, gunmen on Sunday shot dead a leading doctor in the eastern town of Constantine, said Al Khabar newspaper.
Dr Ben Yahia, a member of the Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) led by anti-Islamist hawk Said Saadi, was shot five times in the head in his clinic, it said.
